body.translated_text: Determination of the means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>).

body.text:

children.translated_text: And that <s>pramāṇa</s> is eightfold: <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception), <s>anumāna</s> (inference), <s>āgama</s> (scripture), <s>upamāna</s> (analogy), <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence), <s>sambhava</s> (inclusion), and <s>aitihya</s> (tradition). //

body.translated_text:
Here, correct experience is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).
The word 'correct' (<s>samyak</s>) is for the purpose of excluding doubt (<s>saṃśaya</s>) and error (<s>viparyaya</s>).
Therein, knowledge that does not determine [its object] is doubt.
For example, 'Is this a post or a person?' and so forth.
Error (<s>viparyaya</s>) is a false determination.
For example, 'There are two moons' and the like.
The word 'experience' (<s>anubhava</s>) is for the purpose of excluding memory (<s>smṛti</s>).
Knowledge born solely from impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is memory.
For example, 'She is my mother' and the like.
An impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) is the residual trace of a prior experience.
And that [impression], awakened by the sight of a similar object, is the cause of memory.
But how does the word 'experience' exclude memory, since knowledge other than memory is also experience?
As they say: '<s>Anubhūti</s> (experience) is the <s>pramāṇa</s>; it is other than memory.'
By the word 'solely' [in 'born solely from impressions'], recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) is excluded.
Knowledge born from [both] impression and [present] contact is recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>).
For example, 'This is the very same pot.'
Objection: If only experience is valid knowledge, then how is there the usage of 'means of knowledge' for scripture (<s>āgama</s>) and the like?
We reply: Because they are producers of [valid] knowledge.
As stated by the revered <s>Bhagavatpāda</s> (<s>Śaṅkara</s>): 'Here, the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is what is denoted by the word <s>Upaniṣad</s>.'

children.translated_text:
Nor is it proper [to say] that in 'I,' the <s>ātman</s> alone appears and not the <s>buddhi</s>.
Because, being self-luminous, it cannot be the object of the 'I'-cognition; and because even in deep sleep, fainting, death, and such—where the 'I'-cognition is absent—the <s>ātman</s> continues to shine.
Nor is it proper [to say] that the <s>buddhi</s> alone appears.
Because, being insentient, its appearance is impossible without its fusion with the <s>ātman</s>.
Therefore, it should be accepted that in the [cognition] 'I,' both the <s>buddhi</s> and the <s>ātman</s> appear through mutual identity (<s>tādātmya</s>).
Because pleasure and the like inhere in the <s>buddhi</s> which possesses identity with the <s>ātman</s>, they are apprehended [as] 'I am happy' and so forth.
The apprehension of substances like a pot occurs through the conjunction of the eye—which is a <s>buddhi</s> pervaded by the light of the <s>ātman</s>—[with the object].
Through the inherence-in-the-conjoined of such an eye, there is the apprehension of the color and other [qualities] belonging to it, as in 'This pot is large and white.'
Through the inherence-in-what-inheres-in-the-conjoined of such an eye, there is the apprehension of universals like 'color-ness' residing in the pot's color.
Through the inherence of the ear—which is a <s>buddhi</s> non-different from the <s>ātman</s>—[there is] the apprehension of sound.
Through the inherence-in-what-inheres of such an ear, [there is] the apprehension of universals like 'sound-ness,' as in 'This mountain-cave has a sound.'
Thus, the knowledge of color is through the eye alone.
The knowledge of sound is through the ear alone.
The knowledge of touch is through the skin alone.
The knowledge of taste is through the tongue alone.
The knowledge of smell is through the nose alone.
The knowledge of pleasure and such is through the <s>antaḥkaraṇa</s> (internal organ) alone.
And that [internal organ], in its aspect as <s>manas</s> (mind), is the instrument of the mere appearance of the object.
In its aspect as <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), it is the instrument of the determination of that [object].
In its aspect as <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), it is the cause of the superimposition of that [object] upon the <s>ātman</s>.
In its aspect as <s>citta</s> (thought), it is the instrument of synthesis.
For example: 'This is a pot,' 'This is indeed a pot,' 'I know the pot,' 'The pot has been known by me.'
When the apprehension of color is through the eye alone, the apprehension of the substance that is its substratum is also through that [eye] alone.
So too for the others.
But [the apprehension] of space (<s>vyoman</s>), which is the substratum of sound, is through the mind alone.
page 004

Because of the qualifier-qualified relationship (<s>viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva</s>) of the inherence of a quality in a given substance with its own [corresponding] relations connected to the sense organ, there is apprehension.

children.text: yathā ghaṭe rūpasamavāyaḥ rūpasamavāyavān ghaṭa iti |
children.translated_text: For example: 'The inherence of color in a pot'—'the pot possessing the inherence of color.'
Yogic perception (<s>yogipratyakṣa</s>) is direct knowledge of the reality of the world and what is beyond the world.

Therein, in the state of <s>samādhi</s> (deep meditation), with the mental eye whose veil of darkness has been purified through the power of devotion, knowledge, and <s>yoga</s> practiced continuously over a long period, the apprehension of the non-worldly reality of the <s>ātman</s> alone [takes place], as 'I am <s>Brahman</s>.'

children.text: vyavahāradaśāyāṃ bhoktṛbhogyabhojayitrātmakasya lokālokatattvasya yogaparibhāvitamanaḥsanāthena śāstracakṣuṣā grahaṇam ||
children.translated_text: In the state of ordinary activity (<s>vyavahāra</s>), there is the apprehension of the reality of the world and what is beyond it—consisting of the enjoyer (<s>bhoktṛ</s>), the enjoyed (<s>bhogya</s>), and the controller (<s>bhojayitṛ</s>)—through the eye of scripture (<s>śāstracakṣus</s>), assisted by a mind refined through <s>yoga</s>. //

body.translated_text:
Therein, correct non-mediated experience is perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>).
It is twofold: determinate (<s>savikalpaka</s>) and indeterminate (<s>nirvikalpaka</s>).
Therein, determinate [perception] has as its object a thing qualified by name and other [attributes], as in 'This is a pot.'
Indeterminate [perception] has as its object what is merely delineated [without qualification], as in 'This'—the experience of a bare entity.
That again is twofold: yogic perception (<s>yogipratyakṣa</s>) and non-yogic perception (<s>ayogipratyakṣa</s>).
Therein, non-yogic perception has as its object what is in contact with the sense organs.
And the sense organs are twofold, due to the distinction of external and internal.
The external are the five organs of knowledge (<s>jñānendriya</s>), called ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
The internal are called <s>manas</s> (mind), <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), <s>ahaṅkāra</s> (ego), and <s>citta</s> (thought).
And the objects are twofold, due to the distinction of external and internal.
The external are sound and the like, as well as space (<s>ākāśa</s>) and the like.
The internal are pleasure and the like, as well as <s>buddhi</s> and the like.
The contact of sense organ and object is fivefold: conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), inherence in the conjoined (<s>saṃyuktasamavāya</s>), inherence in what inheres in the conjoined (<s>saṃyuktasamavetasamavāya</s>), inherence (<s>samavāya</s>), and inherence in what inheres (<s>samavetasamavāya</s>).
A sixth relation is characterized by identity (<s>tādātmya</s>).
This [identity relation] is established in the <s>ātman</s> and the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>).
Nor is there any impossibility of identity between the sentient and the insentient.
Because of its being possible by the analogy of wood and fire (<s>kāṣṭhadahana-nyāya</s>).
And because of the relation being due to <s>māyā</s> (illusion), its impossibility is actually an ornament [of the doctrine].
By this [relation], the cognition 'I am this' arises.
Therein, the non-objective aspect (<s>anidamaṃśa</s>) is the <s>ātman</s>, which shines by itself, because consciousness is of a single essence.
The objective aspect (<s>idamaṃśa</s>) is the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), which appears through its fusion with the consciousness of the <s>ātman</s>, being of an insentient nature.
Determination of inference (<s>anumāna</s>).

children.translated_text:
Therein, the statement of the <s>pakṣa</s> (thesis) as possessing the <s>sādhya</s> (thing to be proved) is the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>).
For example: 'This mountain possesses fire.'
The statement of the inferential mark (<s>liṅga</s>) is the reason (<s>hetu</s>).
For example: 'Because of possessing smoke.'
The statement of a correctly observed [instance] is the example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>).
'Whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, like a kitchen'; or 'Whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke, like a lake.'
The application (<s>upanaya</s>) is the statement of pervasion and the pervader with respect to the <s>pakṣa</s>, by way of analogy with the example in which the invariable concomitance of the means and the thing to be proved is well-established.
'And so this [mountain] possesses smoke'; or 'This [lake] is not such—it does not possess smoke.'
The conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>) is the restatement of the thesis together with the reason.
'Therefore it possesses fire'; or 'Therefore it does not possess fire.'
That [inference] again is threefold, due to the distinction of agreement-and-difference (<s>anvayavyatirekin</s>), purely positive (<s>kevalānvayin</s>), and purely negative (<s>kevalavyatirekin</s>).
Therein, the agreement-and-difference [type] has five characteristics (<s>rūpa</s>).
The characteristics are: being a property of the <s>pakṣa</s> (<s>pakṣadharmatva</s>), presence in the homologous instance (<s>sapakṣe sattva</s>), exclusion from the heterologous instance (<s>vipakṣād vyāvṛtti</s>), having an uncontradicted subject (<s>abādhitaviṣayatva</s>), and having no counter-thesis (<s>asatpratipakṣatva</s>).
The <s>pakṣa</s> (subject of the thesis) is the locus qualified by the property to be proved.
Therein, the existence [of the reason] as pervadedly present is the 'being a property of the <s>pakṣa</s>' of the reason.
A locus having properties homogeneous with the <s>sādhya</s> is the <s>sapakṣa</s> (homologous instance).
Presence in all or in some part of it is 'presence in the homologous instance.'
A locus having properties heterogeneous from the <s>sādhya</s> is the <s>vipakṣa</s> (heterologous instance).
The absence of the reason everywhere therein is 'exclusion from the heterologous instance.'
The occurrence of the reason in a subject not contradicted by a <s>pramāṇa</s> is 'having an uncontradicted subject.'
The absence of a counter-thesis is 'having no counter-thesis.'

children.translated_text: The inference based on agreement and difference (<s>anvaya-vyatireka</s>) possesses both the positive concomitance (<s>anvaya-vyāpti</s>) and the negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka-vyāpti</s>) of the reason and the thing to be proved, and is therefore called five-formed. For example: 'The disputed [entity] is false, because of being visible; whatever is visible is false, like a mirage-city etc.; and where [something] is not false, there [it is] not visible, like the self.' The exclusively-positive (<s>kevalānvayin</s>) inference is four-formed, since the counter-instance (<s>vipakṣa</s>) does not exist, and hence exclusion from the counter-instance is absent; for if it were present, the exclusively-positive character would be unestablished. For example: 'The disputed [entity] has a maker, because of being an effect; whatever is an effect has a maker, like a pot.' The exclusively-negative (<s>kevalavyatirekin</s>) inference is also four-formed, since the similar instance (<s>sapakṣa</s>) does not exist, and hence presence in the similar instance is absent. For example: 'Everything that is an effect is preceded by an omniscient maker, because of being an effect; what is not preceded by an omniscient maker is not an effect either, like the self.' And in these inferences, faults of the thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), reason (<s>hetu</s>), and example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>) must be avoided.

children.translated_text: For example [respectively]: 'Fire is hot'; 'fire is not hot'; 'this mountain has tawny fire'; 'the disputed world is false.'

[The faults of the reason are:] being unestablished (<s>asiddha</s>), being contradictory (<s>viruddha</s>), and being deficient (<s>hīna</s>). Thus, an inference that is equipped with three members — from the thesis through the example, or from the thesis through the conclusion — is capable of instructing others.
And that [inference], due to the division of pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>), is established as being threefold.

body.translated_text:
Correct mediated experience through invariable concomitance (<s>avinābhāva</s>) is inference (<s>anumāna</s>).
For example, the knowledge of fire and such from smoke and such, which is pervaded [by fire].
The pervasion (<s>vyāpti</s>) of the means of proof (<s>sādhana</s>) by the thing to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>) by nature is invariable concomitance.
That is twofold, due to the distinction of positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>) and negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>).
Therein, the pervasion of the universal of the means of proof by the universal of the thing to be proved is positive concomitance (<s>anvaya</s>):
'Wherever there is smoke, there is fire.'
The pervasion of the absence of the universal of the thing to be proved by the absence of the universal of the means of proof is negative concomitance (<s>vyatireka</s>):
'Wherever there is no fire, there is also no smoke.'
The word 'correct' (<s>samyak</s>) is for the purpose of excluding [false inference] from steam, mist, and such [which may be mistaken for] fire and so forth.
The word 'mediated' (<s>parokṣa</s>) is for the purpose of excluding perception.
The word 'invariable concomitance' (<s>avinābhāva</s>) is for the purpose of excluding scripture (<s>āgama</s>).
And that is twofold: inference for oneself (<s>svārthānumāna</s>) and inference for others (<s>parārthānumāna</s>).
That which does not depend on instruction from another is inference for oneself.
That which depends on such [instruction] is inference for others.
Instruction for others is a statement having three members.
The members are [either]: thesis (<s>pratijñā</s>), reason (<s>hetu</s>), and example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>); or: example (<s>udāharaṇa</s>), application (<s>upanaya</s>), and conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>).

children.translated_text: Therein, <s>dharma</s>, which is of the nature of impressions (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of meritorious action — even though it is not a self, because it is devoid of form and hence not graspable by the eye and other [senses] — is non-proximate. Because it is the cause of prosperity (<s>abhyudaya</s>) and supreme good (<s>niḥśreyasa</s>), it is a [valid] object. <s>Brahman</s>, because it is the self and the overseer of the senses, and because its being graspable by them is impossible — is non-proximate; because it is of the nature of bliss, it is a [valid] object — this is the distinction. And of these two: because <s>dharma</s> is of a nature beyond direct perception, knowledge of it is indirect (<s>parokṣa</s>). Because <s>Brahman</s> has the nature of the eternal, non-indirect reality of the self, knowledge of it is direct (<s>aparokṣa</s>). Otherwise, knowledge of both would become erroneous. Moreover, by the principle 'what has come into being is taught for the future,' knowledge of <s>dharma</s> is the correct experience of a non-proximate object arising from the verbal [<s>Veda</s>] in the form of injunctions not accompanied [by subsidiary mantras] — since mantras are subordinate [to injunctions]. And by the principle 'what is to come is taught for [understanding] what has been,' knowledge of <s>Brahman</s> is the correct experience of a non-proximate object arising from the verbal [<s>Veda</s>] in the form of the great sentences (<s>mahāvākya</s>), produced by the collection of <s>śrutis</s> in the form of injunctions, explanatory passages (<s>arthavāda</s>), and mantras.

children.translated_text: And <s>dharma</s> is divided into two kinds, as the means of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired. Therein, the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> (new and full moon sacrifices) and others are the means of attaining the desired, such as heaven. The injunction of non-violence toward all beings is the means of avoiding the undesired. Therefore, the means of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired, which are fit to be performed — [that is,] the meaning of injunctions and prohibitions — is not merely an action [to be done]; for in the case of an injunction like 'eat poison,' purposeful agents do not engage [in action]. Nor is it merely the means of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired; for from a statement like 'the moon has risen,' no [purposeful] engagement follows. Even in ordinary statements like 'Child, drink the breast-milk!' or 'Do not touch the fire!' the same principle applies. Thus, the apprehension of verbal capacity (<s>śabda-śakti</s>) too [applies] only to the means of welfare that are fit to be performed, not merely to action. Just as in 'bring the cow,' the apprehension [of the word's meaning applies] only to the means of welfare; just as in 'a son has been born to you,' so is the apprehension. Therefore, regarding the authority of the <s>Vedānta</s> texts concerning the already-established <s>Brahman</s>, there should be no dispute. And injunctive statements are twofold, according to having visible or invisible results. Therein, in the prior section (<s>Pūrvakāṇḍa</s>), the <s>Kārīrī</s> sacrifice and others have visible results. In the latter section (<s>Uttarakāṇḍa</s>), the statements enjoining meditation etc. for the vision of the self have visible results. From perceiving their authoritativeness, the authoritativeness of the others too is to be inferred through the mark of being <s>Veda</s>. And <s>Brahman</s> is twofold, due to the distinction between <s>saguṇa</s> (with attributes) and <s>nirguṇa</s> (without attributes). The <s>saguṇa</s> is also twofold, due to the distinction between the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) and the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>). Therein, the <s>nirguṇa</s> is taught by <s>śruti</s> through characterizations such as truth, knowledge, infinity, etc. The <s>saguṇa</s> pertaining to the Lord is taught through characterizations such as being the cause of the world. That pertaining to the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) is taught through characterizations such as being the one who enters into the created universe. The great sentences (<s>mahāvākya</s>) such as 'That thou art' (<s>Tattvamasi</s>) etc. — supported by those [various texts] that are concerned with purifying the meaning of the words 'that' (<s>tat</s>) [and 'thou' (<s>tvam</s>)] — teach the identity of <s>Brahman</s> and <s>Ātman</s>, which is not known through any other means of knowledge, and whose purpose is the supreme goal of human life (<s>parama-puruṣārtha</s>).

And they teach that from the understanding of that, one attains the highest human goal.
Thus, the <s>Mīmāṃsā</s> treatise was composed for the investigation of the meaning of the <s>Veda</s>, which, being divided into the earlier and later sections, has been accepted by the injunction of study and ascertained as having an intended meaning.
And that [treatise] is bounded by twenty chapters and consists of three sections.
Of these, the <s>Pūrvamīmāṃsā</s> (Earlier Inquiry), measured by twelve chapters, is devoted to the section on ritual action (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>).
Its sūtra-author is <s>Jaimini</s>.
The commentator is <s>Śabarasvāmin</s>.
The two interpreters of that [commentary] are <s>Bhaṭṭa Kumārila</s> and <s>Prabhākara</s>.
Of those two, <s>Bhaṭṭa Kumārila</s> interpreted the injunctive sentences as having <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force) as their purport, while <s>Prabhākara</s> interpreted them as having <s>niyoga</s> (mandate) as their purport.
The <s>Uttaramīmāṃsā</s> (Later Inquiry), however, is of two forms—devoted to <s>Brahman</s> with and without qualities—measured by eight chapters, composed by <s>Vyāsa</s>.
Of these, the portion devoted to <s>Brahman</s> with qualities, consisting of four chapters, constitutes the section on deities (<s>devatākāṇḍa</s>).
Here the commentator is <s>Saṅkarṣa</s>.
In the first chapter, it is established that the purport of all mantras and Vedic distinctions lies in establishing the truth about the deity.
In the second, it is demonstrated that the remainder of the <s>Veda</s>—injunctions, eulogies, and the like—is subsidiary to the mantras and deities.
In the third, it is shown that the nature of the deity is adorned with a host of qualities such as having a form assumed by its own will.
In the fourth, the fruit of worshipping the deity is determined, characterized by the attainment of the respective world, form, adornment, sovereignty, and bliss of each deity through its grace.
Thus, the middle <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, which teaches about <s>Hari</s> as the self of all deities, is devoted to <s>Brahman</s> with qualities.
But the section devoted to <s>Brahman</s> without qualities constitutes the section on knowledge (<s>jñānakāṇḍa</s>).
This too is measured by four chapters.
Its commentator is the blessed <s>Śaṅkarabhagavatpāda</s>.

And partial adherents [of <s>Śaṅkara</s>], such as <s>Brahmadatta</s>, <s>Bhāskara</s>, <s>Rāmānuja</s>, <s>Ānandatīrtha</s>, and others, composed their [respective] pseudo-commentaries on that commentary, each according to their divergent views.
In this, the first chapter demonstrates the consistency of all <s>Vedānta</s> passages with <s>Brahman</s> as the inner self.
By the second, the contradiction from other means of knowledge such as perception and the like is refuted.
By the third, the internal means of attaining the knowledge of <s>Brahman</s>—hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>), reflection (<s>manana</s>), and meditation (<s>nididhyāsana</s>)—are taught together with their foundations.
By the fourth chapter, the fruit of knowledge, characterized as liberation either immediately or gradually, and the fruit of meditation are described.
And liberation is simply the cessation of the ignorance of the self.
Furthermore, for the ignorant person who, setting aside the inquiry into the self, seeks merely the means of attaining pleasure and avoiding pain, the section on ritual action (<s>karmakāṇḍa</s>) was composed.
For one who desires the happiness of the worlds of <s>Brahmā</s>, <s>Viṣṇu</s>, <s>Rudra</s>, <s>Indra</s>, <s>Soma</s>, <s>Sūrya</s>, <s>Vāyu</s>, <s>Agni</s>, and other deities, the section on deities (<s>devatākāṇḍa</s>) was composed.
The section on <s>Brahman</s> (<s>brahmakāṇḍa</s>) was composed with reference to the foremost of persons—one who is detached from all worldly pleasures, who desires only the happiness of liberation from bondage, and who wishes to know the truth of the self. Enough of excessive elaboration.
Because it is devoted to washing away the mud of doubt regarding the invalidity [of the Vedas] cast by the Buddhists and others—through [arguments such as] being the words of an unreliable authority, having mutually contradictory meanings, and the like—and because it determines the definitions of the means of valid knowledge, objects of knowledge, the knower, and so on that are presupposed by those [Vedic sciences], the science of logic (<s>tarkaśāstra</s>) is an auxiliary of the <s>Veda</s>.
And that is of two kinds, distinguished as <s>Naiyāyika</s> (logician) and <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> (atomist).
Of these, the <s>Naiyāyika</s> system, devoted to sixteen categories, was originated by <s>Akṣapāda</s>.
The <s>Vaiśeṣika</s> system, devoted to six categories, was originated by <s>Kaṇāda</s>.
As for the <s>Sāṅkhya</s> system, which is of two kinds—with and without God—it is subsumed under the <s>Itihāsas</s> and <s>Purāṇas</s> and is therefore not counted separately.

Of these, the <s>Nirīśvara Sāṅkhya</s> (Sāṅkhya without God), devoted to twenty-five principles, was authored by <s>Kapila</s>.
The <s>Seśvara Sāṅkhya</s> (Sāṅkhya with God), devoted to twenty-six principles, was composed by <s>Patañjali</s>, by whom the commentary on the grammar of eight chapters composed by <s>Pāṇini</s> was also graced.
Thus there are eighteen branches of knowledge.
All these were bestowed by the Supreme Person upon <s>Brahmā</s> at the beginning of creation.
As stated in the venerable <s>Vāyavīya</s>:
"The four <s>Vedas</s> with their limbs, <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, and the elaborate <s>Nyāya</s>,
the <s>Purāṇa</s> and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>—these are the fourteen branches of knowledge.
<s>Āyurveda</s> (medicine), <s>Dhanurveda</s> (archery), <s>Gāndharvaveda</s> (music) in order,
and the supreme <s>Arthaśāstra</s> (political science) beyond these—thus eighteen branches of knowledge are remembered.
Of these eighteen branches of knowledge, following different paths,
the original author, the Poet, is directly the Trident-bearer (<s>Śūlapāṇi</s>, i.e., <s>Śiva</s>)—so the scripture declares.
For He, the Lord of all the world, wishing to create the entire universe,
first directly produced <s>Brahmā</s> as his eternal son.

Thus.
The experience that arises from the impossibility of any other explanation is <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption).
It is of two kinds, distinguished as based on what is seen and what is heard.
Of these, the ascertainment that the visible movement of the sun from place to place is impossible without locomotion is <s>dṛṣṭārthāpatti</s> (presumption from what is seen).
When it is heard that a momentary sacrifice produces its fruit at another time and place, the ascertainment of the intermediate [entity] <s>apūrva</s> (unseen potency)—because [such a result] is impossible without that [intermediary]—is <s>śrutārthāpatti</s> (presumption from what is heard).
The ascertainment of absence from non-apprehension when the conditions for apprehension are met is <s>abhāvapramāṇa</s> (the means of knowing non-existence).
For example: "There is no pot on this ground."

<s>Saṃbhava</s> (inclusion/possibility) is the ascertainment of a supersensory object arising [from the thought] "this thing is possible."
For example, the ascertainment of the incarnations of <s>Kṛṣṇa</s>, <s>Rāma</s>, and others through the descriptions of the Solar and Lunar dynasties and the like.
<s>Aitihya</s> (tradition) is knowledge arising from a tradition of statements without a specified original speaker.
For example: "A <s>yakṣa</s> dwells in this banyan tree."
Now, how many means of valid knowledge have thus been determined?

For a village-dweller who has asked "what are the characteristics of the animal called <s>gavaya</s> (wild cow)?" and who has received from a forest-dweller the answer "a <s>gavaya</s> is like a cow"—when that person subsequently goes to the forest and by chance sees a <s>gavaya</s>, there arises the perceptual recognition regarding the similarity between the cow and the <s>gavaya</s>: "my cow is similar to this"—that is <s>upamāna</s> (analogy).
As they say:

children.translated_text:
Through this investigation of the means of valid knowledge, the knower and the knowable too are defined.
The knower is the locus of valid knowledge.
The knowable is the object of valid knowledge.
Here, the philosophical treatises are of two kinds, distinguished as Vedic and non-Vedic.
And each of these is of three kinds, distinguished as <s>Mīmāṃsā</s>, <s>Sāṅkhya</s>, and <s>Tarka</s> (logic) [for the Vedic], and <s>Bauddha</s> (Buddhist), <s>Ārhata</s> (Jain), and <s>Lokāyata</s> (Materialist) [for the non-Vedic].
Of these, the first triad is Vedic because it is rooted in the <s>Veda</s>.
The other triad is non-Vedic because it is rooted in pseudo-Vedas composed by the <s>Buddha</s>, the <s>Kṣapaṇaka</s> (Jain ascetic), and <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.
page 015
Thus there are six systems of philosophy (<s>darśanas</s>).

children.translated_text: And thus their statement —
"The fire-sacrifice, the three <s>Vedas</s>, the three-lined [marks], the smearing with ashes —
these are the livelihood of those devoid of intelligence and manly vigor" — thus says <s>Bṛhaspati</s>.

body.translated_text:
Therein, the established doctrine of <s>Cārvāka</s>, the founder of the <s>Lokāyata</s> (materialist) system, who holds that perception alone is the valid means of knowledge, is as follows: Since [we have experiences like] 'I am a person,' 'I am stout,' 'I am thin,' the body itself — the substratum of the quality of consciousness, established through direct perception — is the knowing subject.
The four principles (<s>tattvas</s>) characterized as earth, water, fire, and wind, which by merely coming together in the form of various high and low bodies attain a composite [state] and then again [attain] a dissolved [state], are the objects of knowledge.
<s>Artha</s> (wealth) and <s>kāma</s> (pleasure) alone are the goals of human life (<s>puruṣārtha</s>), not <s>dharma</s> (righteousness).
Only the <s>Arthaveda</s> (science of wealth) and the <s>Gāndharvaveda</s> (science of music), which are grounded in these [two goals], are the [true] <s>Vedas</s>.
Since there is no <s>dharma</s>, there is no <s>adharma</s> (unrighteousness) either.
Therefore, heaven and hell too, being their results, do not exist.
In their absence, there is no supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) who fashions them for embodied beings.
And death itself is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>).
The science of wealth and pleasure, and the <s>Lokāyata</s> science, being rooted in perception, are included within perception alone.
And inference such as 'This food removes hunger, because of being food, like yesterday's food' is also included therein, since it is not different from being rooted in perception.
But the <s>Veda</s>, which concerns <s>dharma</s> and <s>Brahman</s> and has as its fruits worldly prosperity and ultimate good — because it deals with supersensory objects — is simply not a valid means of knowledge. This is the established doctrine.

If those who perform sacrifices [go to] heaven even when the agent, action, and substance perish,

then there should be fruit for abundant trees consumed by forest fire!

and if the <s>Vedāntas</s> are [valid] scriptures, then what wrong have the <s>Buddhists</s> committed?"
And so forth.

And thus the formal argument: the gradation of atomic measure must terminate somewhere, because of being a gradation of measure, like the gradation of large measure [which terminates]. And this world, consisting of the conscious and the non-conscious, is manifold (<s>anekānta</s>).
From the knowledge of that [manifold nature], liberation — characterized by perpetual upward movement — is attained for embodied beings established in <s>dharmas</s> such as non-violence (<s>ahiṃsā</s>). As they say —
"The doctrine of qualified assertion (<s>syādvāda</s>), by abandoning one-sided absolutism in all cases, of the omniscient one,
is conducive to the knowledge of reality through the method of seven-fold predication (<s>saptabhaṅgīnaya</s>)."

children.translated_text:
And the non-absolutism (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>) consists in having an indeterminate form, in the mode of 'exists,' 'does not exist,' and so forth.
And this is established through the method of seven-fold predication (<s>saptabhaṅgīnaya</s>).
How?
'Perhaps it exists' (<s>syād asti</s>), 'perhaps it does not exist' (<s>syān nāsti</s>), 'perhaps it is inexpressible' (<s>syād avaktavya</s>), 'perhaps it exists and does not exist' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti ca</s>), 'perhaps it exists and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti cāvaktavyaṃ ca</s>), 'perhaps it does not exist and is inexpressible' (<s>syān nāsti cāvaktavyaṃ ca</s>), 'perhaps it exists and does not exist and is inexpressible' (<s>syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaṃ ca</s>) — this is the method of seven-fold predication.
The particle 'syāt' (perhaps) indicates non-absolutism.
When asked 'Does the world, consisting of the conscious and non-conscious, exist?' — he says: 'Perhaps it exists.' It is indeterminate as to its existence, because of possessing birth and the like — this is the meaning.
Similarly in 'perhaps it does not exist' and so forth: the indeterminacy of non-existence is because of being experienced [as existent].
The indeterminacy of inexpressibility is because of being denotable by words such as 'blue,' 'pleasure,' and so forth.
The indeterminacy of being of both natures is because, existence and non-existence being contradictory, they cannot co-exist in a single locus.
The indeterminacy of 'it exists and is inexpressible' is because it is fit to be said 'it does not exist' as well.
The indeterminacy of

'it does not exist and is inexpressible' is because it is fit to be said 'it exists' as well.
The indeterminacy of 'it exists and does not exist and is inexpressible' is because it is fit to be said both 'it exists' and 'it does not exist.'
Thus, having ascertained that the universe is devoid of any absolute state, the person who has thereupon attained <s>nirveda</s> (world-weariness), through the power of <s>yoga</s>, attains liberation characterized by perpetual upward movement.

body.translated_text:
Among the <s>Kṣapaṇaka</s> (Jain) and the <s>Bauddha</s> (Buddhist), who hold perception and inference as valid means of knowledge, the established doctrine of the <s>Kṣapaṇaka</s> is as follows: From the experience 'this is my body,' the body has a seer distinct from itself — [established] through inference: 'because of being visible, or because of being material, like a pot.' And because <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), movement, consciousness, memory, and the like are not found in a dead body, the knowing subject, called the <s>ātman</s> (self), distinct from the body, is a special luminous substance of either the body's measure or atomic measure.
[The objection] 'supersensory objects should not be accepted, because of over-extension' is not valid — because the validity of perception [itself], being supersensory, would [also] have to be accepted [as supersensory].
Therefore, by the authority of the scripture composed by the <s>Arhat</s> sages, <s>dharma</s> (merit), <s>adharma</s> (demerit), heaven, and hell also exist.
The <s>dharmas</s> (meritorious practices) are: plucking of hair, wandering for alms, carrying a peacock-feather [broom], celibacy, fasting, non-covering [of the body], bathing without [cosmetics], bowing to the <s>Arhat</s>, ascending heated stones, and the like.
But the <s>Vedic</s> rites such as the fire-sacrifice are merely semblances of <s>dharma</s>, because they are accomplished through the harming of sentient beings, both moving and stationary.
And because the invalidity of the <s>Veda</s> is ascertained through [its] not being the utterance of a trustworthy person, through internally contradictory meanings, and so forth.
<s>Adharma</s> (demerit) is characterized by violence to living beings (<s>prāṇihiṃsā</s>) and the like.
The bodies of moving and stationary beings, together with their causes, are the objects of knowledge — these are constructed from atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) of earth, water, fire, and air, also called <s>pudgalas</s> (material particles), impelled by the <s>karmas</s> of living beings designated as <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s>.
And atoms are established through inference.
Exposition of the Buddhist (<s>Sugata</s>) doctrine.

Conventional reality (<s>saṃvṛtti</s>) is a category (<s>padārtha</s>) whose own-characteristic is inexpressible as existent, non-existent, or otherwise, which is the cause of the non-existent appearing as existent.
Therefore, the triad of knower and the rest is in reality non-existent but appears as existent. For one who serves the teacher <s>Sugata</s> (Buddha), attended by the five <s>Buddhas</s>, with mind, speech, and body, and who meditates continuously for a long time [on the truth] that 'everything is empty' — when the mind of that good person dissolves into the void, liberation characterized by the attainment of total emptiness will be achieved. This is the established doctrine.
The <s>Yogācāra</s>, who comes after [the Mādhyamika], holds — if the knower is non-existent, then the establishment of the empty object of knowledge simply does not occur; therefore some knower must be accepted.
And it is self-luminous (<s>svaprakāśa</s>);
otherwise there would follow the need for yet another establisher.
And self-luminosity is not conceivable for anything other than consciousness (<s>jñāna</s>). Therefore, [it is established] through direct perception that 'I am,' and through inference that 'the body is not the self, because of being visible, like a pot' — the <s>ālayavijñāna</s> (store-consciousness), which perishes moment by moment and arises [anew], is the knowing subject.
The impression of stability in it is due to the stability of the stream [of consciousness].
[The thought] 'I who saw an elephant in the morning — that same I, now having seen the mass of darkness, remember it' — this is simply an error, like [saying] 'this is the [same] flame.'
The five <s>skandhas</s> (aggregates), called <s>rūpa</s> (form), <s>vijñāna</s> (consciousness), <s>vedanā</s> (feeling), <s>saṃjñā</s> (perception), and <s>saṃskāra</s> (formations), dissolving and arising moment by moment in accordance with the <s>karmas</s> of living beings, undergoing transformation and cessation in the form of gods, humans, and hell-beings by their own nature — these are the objects of knowledge.
Among them, the sense-faculties and their objects constitute the <s>rūpa-skandha</s> (form-aggregate).
The knowledge arising therefrom is the <s>vijñāna-skandha</s> (consciousness-aggregate).
Its result — pleasure, pain, and delusion — is the <s>vedanā-skandha</s> (feeling-aggregate).
Cognitions qualified by name, quality, action, and genus constitute the <s>saṃjñā-skandha</s> (perception-aggregate).
Here, 'cow,' 'horse,' 'person' and the like are <s>saṃjñā</s> (names).
'Cow-ness,' 'horse-ness,' 'person-ness' and the like are <s>jāti</s> (genus).

children.translated_text: White, red, black, etc. — these are qualities (<s>guṇa</s>). Standing, going, sitting, etc. — these are actions (<s>kriyā</s>). 'Having horns, four-footed, having a tail,' etc. — these are qualified cognitions (<s>viśiṣṭapratyaya</s>). The aggregate of dispositions (<s>saṃskāra-skandha</s>) is characterized by momentum (<s>vega</s>), coiling (<s>veṣṭana</s>), steadying (<s>sthitasthāpaka</s>), etc. Momentum belongs to arrows and the like; coiling to birch-bark and the like; steadying to branches and the like. That which has the above-stated characteristics is the object of valid knowledge (<s>prameya</s>). If that [object] is other than cognition (<s>prakāśa</s>), then it would never be cognized at all — therefore everything is merely of the nature of cognition (<s>jñānākāra</s>). If cognition were stable, [objects like] blue, yellow, etc. would appear to everyone at all times, [but] they do not [always appear] to anyone — therefore [cognition] itself is unstable. Hence this entire world, consisting of the grasped (<s>grāhya</s>), the grasper (<s>grāhaka</s>), and the grasping (<s>grahaṇa</s>), is forever submerged in the continuum (<s>santāna</s>) of the store-consciousness (<s>ālayavijñāna</s>) as 'I.' Therefore, for a person who is devoted to the true <s>Dharma</s> — through worshipping <s>caityas</s> (shrines), [recollecting] the <s>Buddha</s>, and practicing, etc. — and who has long meditated [on the view that] all this is mere consciousness (<s>vijñāna</s>), liberation in the form of the arising of a purified consciousness-continuum is established right here — this is the established doctrine. Therefore, since the more recent [school's] student, called <s>Sautrāntika</s>, [holds that] because of the impossibility of causal efficacy (<s>arthakriyākāritva</s>) when the universe exists internally but not externally, because of the undesirable consequence of the reversal of error and its sublation, and because of the undesirable consequence of insentience (<s>jaḍatva</s>) if cognition took the form of the knowable — the separateness of the two must be accepted; thus the universe is both external and internal. And if that [universe] were stable, the observed transition of a seed through the states of swelling, sprouting, becoming a tree, leafing, flowering, fruiting, etc. would not be coherent — therefore momentary particular characteristics (<s>kṣaṇika-svalakṣaṇa</s>) must be accepted. Similarly, if the knower were stable, then because cognition too would be stable, one would always cognize blue and never yellow, or vice versa. Therefore the knower too is unstable. This is the distinction: internal cognition (<s>jñāna</s>) is a particular characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>) that is directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>); the external [object] such as blue etc. is only inferred (<s>anumeya</s>).

children.translated_text: That is as follows: in cognition, the reflection (<s>pratibimba</s>) of the knowable is preceded by the original (<s>bimba</s>); because it is a reflection, like the reflection of a face in a mirror. And thus there is no externally existing object grasped by perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>). [According to] the most recent student of the <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>: the external object, being present, is directly perceived (<s>pratyakṣa</s>), because in [the cognition] 'this is blue,' it is seen appearing with directness (<s>aparokṣatā</s>) alone. Therefore between these two [schools] there is only this difference; everything else is the same. And among these positions, since the teachings (<s>āgama</s>) of <s>Buddha</s> etc. are grounded in inference (<s>anumāna</s>) and are subsumed therein, there is no additional means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>). Among these, for the <s>Sautrāntika</s> and <s>Vaibhāṣika</s>, having understood through scripture (<s>śāstra</s>) that everything is momentary (<s>kṣaṇika</s>), while serving the <s>Bhagavān</s> <s>Tathāgata</s>, the Teacher, and his devotees — when direct realization (<s>sākṣādbodha</s>) of the momentariness of everything arises, one attains liberation in the form of obtaining a purified consciousness-continuum — this is the established doctrine. Of all three of these [Buddhist schools], at bottom, the doctrine is of emptiness (<s>śūnyavāda</s>). How?
The <s>Yogācāra</s> declares the emptiness (<s>śūnyatva</s>) of external objects.
The <s>Sautrāntika</s> [declares] the emptiness of directly perceived external objects.

children.translated_text: Here is the summary [verse]: 'The principal <s>Mādhyamika</s> considered the entire world as a transformation (<s>vivarta</s>) of the void (<s>śūnya</s>). In the <s>Yogācāra</s> view, cognitions indeed exist, and the entire [external world] is their transformation. The <s>Sautrāntika</s> [holds that] the object exists but is momentary and is inferred through cognition. The <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> declares that everything is momentary and directly perceived.'

Since, if the <s>ātman</s> were of atomic measure, the simultaneous awareness and continuity of sensations in all the limbs would be impossible; since, if it were of the body's measure, knowledge of external objects would be impossible and there would follow impermanence like a pot; since, if everything were non-absolute, the non-absoluteness itself would [have to be] likewise; since, by the maxim 'all elevations end in falling,' liberation in the form of perpetual upward movement, ending in falling, would not be established as an eternal human goal — since this [Jaina] position is not free from defects, the <s>Sugata</s> (Buddhist) doctrine is now commenced.
This [doctrine] is divided into four according to the differences of disciples.
The disciples — <s>Mādhyamika</s>, <s>Yogācāra</s>, <s>Sautrāntika</s>, and <s>Vaibhāṣika</s> — are progressively distinguished by degrees of purity.
Among them, the <s>Mādhyamika</s>, who is the student of the highest qualification — the knowing subject is of empty nature (<s>śūnya-svabhāva</s>), as seen from the memory of one waking from sleep: 'I was void for this much time.'
Further, the cognition of existence regarding the self — 'I am' — pertains to conventional reality (<s>saṃvṛttitattva</s>) alone.
Similarly the cognition 'the pot exists' and so forth.
Therefore the object of knowledge too is simply empty, because the destruction of what [truly] exists is impossible.
Likewise the means of valid knowledge is in reality simply empty, because birth and destruction are impossible for what [truly] exists.
The cognition of existence is merely conventional.
Thus. ||

children.translated_text: And it is divided twenty-four-fold according to the division into: color (<s>rūpa</s>), taste (<s>rasa</s>), smell (<s>gandha</s>), touch (<s>sparśa</s>), number (<s>saṃkhyā</s>), measure (<s>parimāṇa</s>), separateness (<s>pṛthaktva</s>), conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), disjunction (<s>vibhāga</s>), remoteness (<s>paratva</s>), proximity (<s>aparatva</s>), heaviness (<s>gurutva</s>), fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>), viscosity (<s>sneha</s>), cognition (<s>buddhi</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), effort (<s>prayatna</s>), merit (<s>dharma</s>), demerit (<s>adharma</s>), disposition (<s>saṃskāra</s>), and sound (<s>śabda</s>). Among these, the qualities of earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>) are: color, taste, smell, touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, heaviness, caused fluidity, and disposition. Water (<s>ap</s>) possesses the said qualities along with viscosity (<s>sneha</s>) but without smell. The qualities of fire (<s>tejas</s>) are: color, touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, caused fluidity, and disposition. The qualities of air (<s>vāyu</s>) are: touch, number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, velocity (<s>vega</s>), and disposition. The qualities of ether (<s>ākāśa</s>) are: number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, and sound. The qualities of time (<s>kāla</s>) are: number, measure, separateness, conjunction, and disjunction. And the same are the qualities of direction (<s>dik</s>). The qualities of the self (<s>ātman</s>) are: number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and disposition. The qualities of mind (<s>manas</s>) are: number, measure, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, remoteness, proximity, velocity, and disposition. The nine special qualities of the self are cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) etc. The special quality of ether is sound. Of air, touch. Of fire, color. Of water, taste. Of earth, smell. Direction, time, and mind have no special qualities. Action (<s>karma</s>) is of the same class as the non-inherent cause of conjunction and disjunction. It is fivefold, according to the division into: throwing upward (<s>utkṣepaṇa</s>), throwing downward (<s>avakṣepaṇa</s>), contraction (<s>ākuñcana</s>), expansion (<s>prasāraṇa</s>), and locomotion (<s>gamana</s>). Universal (<s>sāmānya</s>) is eternal and present in many [instances]. It is twofold: higher (<s>para</s>) and lower (<s>apara</s>). The higher is existence (<s>sattā</s>), because of its occurrence in more [things]. The lower is substance-ness (<s>dravyatva</s>) etc., because of its occurrence in fewer [things]. Particularities (<s>viśeṣa</s>) are eternal, reside in eternal [substances], are the causes of cognitions of absolute distinction, and are infinite and ultimate.

That [scripture] by which the accepted meaning is conveyed is the <s>Veda</s>; and it is composed by the Supreme Lord who possesses eternal will, knowledge, and the power of action; having created the universe consisting of words and meanings, and having established the convention of word-power—'this word has this meaning'—[He] promulgated [the <s>Veda</s>] for the purpose of the prosperity and supreme good of living beings. And the existence of <s>Īśvara</s> (God) is ascertained through inference:

Nor is it proper [to say] that all effects arise from nature (<s>svabhāva</s>) alone.

Therefore, because an effect necessarily requires a cause, and because the universe is established as an effect due to having parts, its cause must be inferred.
A cause is a definite antecedent.
It is threefold, due to the distinction of <s>samavāyi</s> (material cause), <s>asamavāyi</s> (non-material cause), and <s>nimitta</s> (efficient cause).
The material cause (<s>samavāyikāraṇa</s>) is that in which the effect inheres.
For example: clay is [the material cause] of a pot.
The non-material cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>) is that which is proximate to the material cause and whose capacity has been ascertained.
For example: the mutual conjunction of the parts of clay.
The efficient cause (<s>nimittakāraṇa</s>) is that which is other than the material and non-material causes and whose capacity has been ascertained.
For example: the potter's stick, wheel, and the like.
Therein, in the production of the universe, atoms are the material cause.
Their mutual conjunction is the non-material cause.
The Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>) is the efficient cause.
And creation is the connection with being (<s>sattā</s>) of what was previously non-existent.
Because the created universe consists of pleasure and pain, the <s>karmas</s> (actions) of living beings are also efficient causes here—this is the gist.
The <s>śruti</s> passages such as 'From which indeed...' and the <s>smṛti</s> passages such as 'I am the first...' and the like, as well as [passages like] 'His supreme power...'—these are of the nature of inference of eternal will, knowledge, and effort.
The same reasoning applies to other <s>śrutis</s> as well.
The <s>śruti</s> sentences such as 'By the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>...' are of the nature of inference.
For by them, it is revealed that the acts of worshipping the Supreme Lord such as the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> and the like are means of attaining fruits such as heaven.
Therein, the reasoning is as follows: 'The disputed ritual acts such as sacrifice are means of attaining the desired fruit, because of being service to the Lord, like service to a worldly sovereign.'
Similarly, the sentences enjoining hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>) and the like for the vision of the Self [are of inferential nature].
For they reveal that listening to [teachings about] the Supreme Self and the like are means of liberation characterized by the cessation of all suffering, through the door of producing the grace of that [Lord].

body.translated_text: Here, [the Buddhist positions are refuted as follows:] because the world's having an empty nature (<s>śūnyasvabhāva</s>) entails the undesirable consequence of non-establishment due to the absence of proofs; because of the contradiction with the experience of existence; because if cognition took the form of the knowable, insentience (<s>jaḍatva</s>) would follow; because of the undesirable consequence of external non-perception of the knowable; because if blue, which appears directly as 'this,' were inferential, then the cognition's own particular characteristic (<s>svalakṣaṇa</s>), which appears as 'I,' would also hypothetically become inferential; because if the knower were unstable, memory (<s>smṛti</s>), which is directed toward previously experienced objects, would be impossible; because if the knowable were momentary, recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) — 'this is the same pot' — would be impossible; because even though cognitions of objects like blue etc., which are modifications of <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), arise and perish, the witness-consciousness (<s>sākṣi-caitanya</s>) underlying <s>buddhi</s> remains stable; because without coloring by objects, cognition, lacking a differentiator, cannot constitute a continuum (<s>santāna</s>); and because, being self-luminous (<s>svaprakāśa</s>), the impossibility of apprehending its birth and destruction either by itself or by another [entails that] its non-existence cannot be established for something whose [nature] is unapprehended — therefore, like the positions of the <s>Jains</s> etc., the <s>Buddhist</s> position too should be set aside. And since even though [<s>Kaṇāda</s>] is a proponent of Vedic authority, he accepts [Vedic authority] as having the nature of inference — therefore the view of <s>Kaṇāda</s>, who is subsumed among those who accept only perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>) as means of valid knowledge, is now introduced. Here, substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), particularity (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>) — these are the six categories (<s>padārthas</s>) alone. Among these, substance (<s>dravya</s>) is that which possesses qualities. It is divided ninefold: according to the division into earth (<s>pṛthivī</s>), water (<s>ap</s>), fire (<s>tejas</s>), air (<s>vāyu</s>), ether (<s>ākāśa</s>), time (<s>kāla</s>), direction (<s>dik</s>), self (<s>ātman</s>), and mind (<s>manas</s>). Among these, the eighth substance called self (<s>ātman</s>) is the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>). And he is different from the bodies etc. which are characterized as earth etc., eternal (<s>nitya</s>), all-pervading (<s>vibhu</s>), different in each body, dependent on the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>), insentient (<s>jaḍa</s>) by nature, and grasped by the cognition 'I.' The other substances and the qualities etc. are the objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>). A quality (<s>guṇa</s>) is that which possesses a universal, which has no non-inherent cause (<s>asamavāyikāraṇa</s>), and which is without motion (<s>aspanda</s>).

The postulations of <s>Akṣapāda</s>, who accepts perception, inference, scripture, and analogy as means of valid knowledge, are as follows—similar to <s>Kaṇāda</s>: the postulation of the knower, the postulation of the Supreme Lord as different from the knower, the postulation that knowers are many, eternal, all-pervading, and possessed of qualities such as knowledge, the postulation of [the self's] insentience, the postulation of [the self] being knowable through the 'I'-cognition, the postulation of the <s>Veda</s>, the postulation of eternal and non-eternal [entities] among the knowables, the postulation that atoms are the producers of the universe, the postulation of the three human goals beginning with <s>dharma</s>, the postulation of bondage and liberation, and the postulation that darkness is not a separate substance but merely the absence of light.
This is the [only] difference: <s>Akṣapāda</s>, without distinction, is a proponent of sixteen categories.
Thus his sūtra: 'From the true knowledge of the sixteen categories—<s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge), <s>prameya</s> (objects of knowledge), <s>saṃśaya</s> (doubt), <s>prayojana</s> (purpose), <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example), <s>siddhānta</s> (established conclusion), <s>avayava</s> (members of syllogism), <s>tarka</s> (hypothetical reasoning), <s>nirṇaya</s> (ascertainment), <s>vāda</s> (debate), <s>jalpa</s> (wrangling), <s>vitaṇḍā</s> (cavil), <s>hetvābhāsa</s> (fallacious reasons), <s>chala</s> (quibbling), <s>jāti</s> (futile rejoinder), and <s>nigrahasthāna</s> (points of defeat)—the highest good is attained.'

children.translated_text: Nor is there here the fault that the validity of perception and the like depends on the absence of sublation — because the validity characterized as 'making known what was previously unknown' does not apply to erroneous cognitions and the like. Nor does the object of error etc. exist in the prior and subsequent moments, such that it would remain as unknown. By this very reasoning, the invalidity of memory should be inferred. Now, for one who considers validity to be of the nature of absence of sublation — how can memory be invalid? For no subsequent sublation of it is seen. Therefore, in accepting erroneous and doubtful cognitions, there is no fault whatsoever. The <s>puruṣa</s> (person/self), whose nature is consciousness that is eternally arisen, never setting, and objectless, is the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) — this is common to both the atheistic (<s>nirīśvara</s>) and theistic (<s>seśvara</s>) [Sāṅkhya]. The theistic [school] considers this [<s>puruṣa</s>] to be twofold through the distinction of individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) and supreme [soul] (<s>para</s>). And it determines a threefold [division] in the individual soul through the distinctions of god (<s>sura</s>), human (<s>nara</s>), and hell-being (<s>nāraka</s>). In both schools, since the <s>puruṣa</s> is immutable (<s>kūṭastha</s>), it is <s>Prakṛti</s> (primordial nature) — composed of the three <s>guṇas</s>: <s>sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> — that alone transforms into the form of the world; and the created world's nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is accepted. For the atheistic [Sāṅkhya], the principles (<s>tattvas</s>) are twenty-five: <s>puruṣa</s>, <s>prakṛti</s>, <s>mahat</s> (the great [principle]), <s>ahaṃkāra</s> (ego), <s>manas</s> (mind), the five sense-organs (ear, skin, eye, tongue, nose), the five action-organs (speech, hands, feet, excretory organ, generative organ), the five subtle elements (sound, touch, form, taste, smell), and the five gross elements (space, wind, fire, water, earth).

children.translated_text: In both [schools], <s>dharmas</s> characterized by engagement (<s>pravṛtti</s>) and withdrawal (<s>nivṛtti</s>) include the fire-sacrifice, <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, and the like, as well as the restraints (<s>yama</s>), observances (<s>niyama</s>), and the like. Engagement-characterized [dharma] is the cause of <s>saṃsāra</s>. Withdrawal-characterized [dharma] is the cause of liberation through the door of knowledge of reality. This is the specific difference: for the theistic [Sāṅkhya], <s>yoga</s> assisted by knowledge of reality is the cause of liberation; for the other [atheistic Sāṅkhya], knowledge of reality assisted by <s>yoga</s> is the cause of liberation. The limbs of <s>yoga</s> are: <s>yama</s> (restraint), <s>niyama</s> (observance), <s>āsana</s> (posture), <s>prāṇāyāma</s> (breath control), <s>pratyāhāra</s> (withdrawal of senses), <s>dhāraṇā</s> (concentration), <s>dhyāna</s> (meditation), and <s>samādhi</s> (absorption). And the fruits of <s>yoga</s> are of two kinds, according to the distinction between knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>) and ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>). Therein, those born of knowledge are devotion (<s>bhakti</s>), wisdom (<s>jñāna</s>), and dispassion (<s>vairāgya</s>). Those born of ignorance are the eight supernatural powers (<s>aiśvarya</s>) beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (becoming minute). Likewise there are also other external <s>yoga</s> powers. As they say:

body.translated_text: In all three of these positions [Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, and variant Nyāya]: because of the impossibility of being a knower when the self is insentient; because of the absurdity of being subject to modification when [the self] is the substratum of qualities like <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) etc.; because of the absurdity that the Supreme Lord would be insentient if He is different from a conscious being; and because the identity with consciousness is impossible to be grasped either independently or dependently; because when the self is knowable through the 'I'-cognition, the impossibility of its being insentient like a pot is not averted; because if cognitions are knowable by subsequent reflective cognitions (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>), and if these are admitted to be self-luminous, there arises the fallacy of a pseudo-established-conclusion (<s>apasiddhānta</s>); if they are illumined by another [cognition], there is an infinite regress; if they are knowable [as objects], they cannot be cognitions; because if the <s>Veda</s> is of human authorship, there is the absurd consequence of requiring a prior fundamental <s>pramāṇa</s>; because if God possesses eternal will and the like, there is the absurd consequence of His having an eternal body; because if liberation is of the nature of the cessation of nine qualities, there is the absurd consequence of being equivalent to a stone; because if happiness is [merely] the absence of suffering, the establishment of the conscious being as the substratum of nine qualities fails, since one could equally say 'the absence of happiness is suffering';

body.translated_text: And so on. Here, for the theistic [school], through <s>yoga</s> combined with knowledge of reality, the <s>yogin's</s> attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>) is liberation. For the atheistic [school], through knowledge combined with <s>yoga</s>, the gain of discrimination between <s>Prakṛti</s> and <s>Puruṣa</s> is liberation. Now, in the theistic school, what is the superiority of the Supreme <s>Puruṣa</s> over the individual soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>)? <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord) is a special <s>puruṣa</s> untouched by afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), actions (<s>karma</s>), results of actions (<s>vipāka</s>), and latent impressions (<s>āśaya</s>); the individual soul (<s>kṣetrajña</s>) is one who is entangled with afflictions and the rest.

children.translated_text: Therein, the horn of a hare is an example of absolute absence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>). The prior non-existence (<s>prāgabhāva</s>) of pots etc. [exists] before their production. Posterior non-existence (<s>pradhvaṃsa</s>) [exists] after destruction. The mutual absence (<s>anyonyābhāva</s>) is the non-identity of a pot with cloth etc. The absence of connection (<s>saṃsargābhāva</s>) is [e.g.] the absence of a monkey in a place [where monkeys are not found]. And darkness is a separate substance, not merely the absence of light, nor merely the absence of perception of form. Why? Because of the contradiction with <s>śruti</s> passages such as 'there was darkness.' Furthermore, if [darkness were] the absence of light — is darkness the absence of one light or the absence of all lights? In the first case, [darkness] would always be perceived, since the absence of one light is possible always and everywhere. In the second case, darkness would never be perceived at all, since the absence of all lights is impossible anywhere. Similarly, the view that [darkness is] absence of perception of form should be refuted. If darkness, which is perceived as an existent entity, is imagined to be a non-existence, then how could the imagination of light as a non-existence of darkness be prevented? And for the teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>], who does not accept non-existence — since the absence of perception of form also does not exist — how could the claim that darkness is of that nature be consistent?

children.text: abhāvajñānasya nirviṣayatvaṃ vadannasau bhāvajñānasya nirālambanatvaṃ sādhayantaṃ mādhyamikaṃ vā kathaṃ nirākuryāt |
children.translated_text: And how could he, who says that the cognition of absence has no object, refute the <s>Mādhyamika</s> [Buddhist] who establishes that the cognition of existents too has no foundation (<s>nirālambana</s>)?
Therefore this [position of Prabhākara] amounts to something trivial.

children.translated_text: As stated by <s>Bhaṭṭapāda</s> [<s>Kumārila</s>]: 'Darkness indeed is moving, dark blue, and possessing the distinction of far and near;
It deserves to be distinguished from the nine [established] substances on the grounds of dissimilarity with well-known substances.'

body.translated_text: Although <s>Prabhākara</s>, who advocates the validity of four means of knowledge including presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) along with perception etc., and <s>Bhaṭṭa Kumārila</s>, who advocates the validity of five means of knowledge including non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) along with perception etc., are alike in being commentators on the <s>Jaiminīya Bhāṣya</s> — there is a disagreement regarding the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>) and the knowable (<s>prameya</s>) comparable to [their agreement on] the means of knowledge. How so? For the teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>], for whom non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) is not a valid means of knowledge, non-existence is simply not any kind of object at all. Rather, in 'there is no pot on this ground,' only the bare ground alone is cognized; and darkness is merely the absence of perception of form — not a separate substance. But for <s>Kumārila</s>, for whom non-existence is a valid means of knowledge, even the object characterized by absence exists. And it is fivefold, due to the distinctions of absolute absence (<s>atyantābhāva</s>) etc.

children.translated_text: Or [their] validity only in some way as subordinate to injunctions (<s>vidhiśeṣa</s>); the eternality of the celestial, terrestrial, and netherworld realms; the absence of a Lord (<s>nirīśvaratva</s>); the multiplicity, reality, and [separate] existence of the universe consisting of the conscious and the non-conscious; the deities such as <s>Indra</s>, <s>Agni</s>, etc. being merely words ending in the dative case, without possessing the five forms [of body]; <s>dharma</s> being of the nature of the fire-sacrifice, <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s>, animal sacrifice, <s>Soma</s> sacrifice, and the like; and liberation being of the nature of the self remaining in its own essential nature — [all this] is common to the teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>] and <s>Kumārila</s>. The following is their difference: For the teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>], all cognitions are veridical, since erroneous and doubtful cognitions are merely non-discrimination. And recognition (<s>pratyabhijñā</s>) is included within experience (<s>anubhava</s>) itself, as apprehending a persisting [object] such as a pot etc. that was previously unknown — hence cognition is simply a twofold collection of the nature of apprehension and memory. And their self-luminosity (<s>svaprakāśatva</s>) [is accepted], like the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> etc. — because if cognition were knowable by another cognition, that [other cognition] too would be likewise, leading to an infinite regress; and because if [cognition were] a knowable [object], there would be the undesirable consequence of its being insentient like a pot. The self, however, like the <s>Vaiśeṣikas</s> etc., is a special insentient substance (<s>jaḍa-dravya-viśeṣa</s>), the substrate of properties like cognition etc., and hence different from the body etc., eternal, all-pervading, wandering through the three worlds due to <s>karma</s>, established through means of knowledge such as perception, and having the nature of being an agent and experiencer. Even though it is insentient, because of illuminating [objects] through being the substrate of cognition, it has the status of a knower. Because of being illuminated as the object [of cognition], a pot has the status of a knowable. Thus, in 'I know the pot,' cognition [is known] by itself; the knower [is illuminated] through being the substrate of that [cognition]; and the pot through being the object of that — thus the teacher [<s>Prabhākara</s>] speaks of the triplet-perception (<s>tripuṭī-pratyakṣa</s>). And thus his statement:
"The self, different from cognition, the sense organs, and the body, is all-pervading and eternal;
Being manifold — one for each body — it shines upon the substrates of objects."
Thus.

And difference is simply the own-nature [of a thing] that does not depend on another—it is not an attribute.
Otherwise there would be the absurd consequence of requiring yet another difference [ad infinitum].
The meaning of an injunctive [sentence] is simply <s>niyoga</s> (mandate), having sacrificial rites and the like as its objects.
Since that [mandate] is not amenable to any other means of valid knowledge, it is called <s>apūrva</s> (unseen potency); because it is accomplishable by effort, it is called <s>kārya</s> (duty); and because it is the aim of effort, it is called <s>pradhāna</s> (principal).
But the fact that it confers fruits such as heaven upon the person mandated by its own [Vedic] authority does not compromise [the mandate's] independence.
Therefore, in the sentence "One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>," the mandate (<s>niyoga</s>) is understood through the optative verbal suffix (<s>liṅ</s>) in "should sacrifice" (<s>yajeta</s>).
Just like the royal command "One who desires a comfortable dwelling should serve me."
And since that [mandate] is well-known as being of someone, in some domain—through the verbal root <s>yaj</s> (to sacrifice), the domain is indicated; and through "one who desires heaven," the person mandated is specified.
Through the instrumental case-ending in "with the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>," the specification of which sacrifice the mandate pertains to is supplied, and through the qualifier "desiring heaven" of the qualified person, the specification of the mandated person is also made.
Therefore the meaning is: the mandate for one who desires heaven is in the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> sacrifice.
Other injunctions too, by the principle 'In the proximity of [an injunction] with a fruit, what lacks a fruit is a subsidiary of that'—are injunctions subsidiary to this.
And mantras, being reminders of the performance, partake of this subsidiary status.
Eulogistic passages (<s>arthavādas</s>), being revealers of the praise of the fruit, also assist the injunction by producing the desire to perform the mandate that accomplishes [the fruit].
The same principle applies in other cases as well.

children.translated_text:
Even more advanced than the teacher is <s>Kumārila</s>, [who holds that] cognitions are of many kinds—distinguished as experience, memory, and recognition; and within experience itself, distinguished as valid, erroneous, and doubtful—like <s>Kaṇāda</s>, <s>Akṣapāda</s>, <s>Patañjali</s>, and others.
The knower is of the nature of a substance possessing consciousness, and has perception, inference, presumption, and scripture as valid means of knowledge.
Because of having a nature different from the object of knowledge, it has the character of ignorance [as its ground]; because of being the substratum of qualities such as cognition, it is a substance.
Nor should it be said that since the substance that is the locus of knowledge is different from knowledge, a connection with knowledge is impossible—because even the solar disc, which is different from light, is seen to possess luminosity, since it is the cause of illumination.
And because without the form of being both inert and non-inert, it is not established as the object of the cognition "I."
As for what is said—that erroneous cognitions have the nature of non-discrimination—that is weak.
Because for one who accepts [the theory of] <s>akhyāti</s> (non-apprehension of difference) and holds non-discrimination to be of the nature of the absence of discrimination, it is unfitting to speak of non-discrimination.
Between what two things here is non-discrimination?
If between apprehension and memory—no.
Because the experience "This is silver" has the nature of an experience of identity with the silver present before one, and therefore is not an error.
Rather, for a person who possesses the impression from [a prior] experience of silver, due to a defect in the instrument such as defective vision and a defect in the object such as similarity, when the shell-fragment is grasped merely as something white and gleaming—its appearing with the nature of remembered silver is the error.
And cognitions of pots, pleasure, and the like are knowable through introspective cognition (<s>anuvyavasāya</s>).
Because the cognition "this is a pot" is made the object of a subsequent cognition "I know the pot."
Nor is there an infinite regress here, because there is no desire for further inquiry beyond the seer.
And difference is not merely the own-nature of the different thing—because the word 'difference' would then become a synonym of words like 'pot,' and because difference, which is established in dependence on another, cannot be the own-nature [of a thing].

Nor is there the fault of requiring yet another difference when [difference] is an attribute of the different—because, like the self, it is capable of accomplishing both itself and another.
For the self, while knowing all things, also knows itself.
And <s>bhāvanā</s> (productive force) is the meaning of an injunction.
And it has three aspects: 'what,' 'by what means,' and 'how.'
To fill the 'what' aspect, the word 'one who desires heaven' [is used].
To fill the 'by what means' aspect, the verbal root <s>yaj</s> (to sacrifice) [is used] as the base.
To specify that, the expression 'by the <s>Agniṣṭoma</s>' [is used] as the base.
The suffix-portion, characterized by the third case-ending, serves to indicate its instrumentality.
Nor is it impossible for the momentary sacrifice to be the means of a fruit [arising] at a later time—because that is possible through the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) inherent in the sacrificer himself.
The subsidiary injunctions such as those for the preliminary offerings (<s>prayājas</s>) and the like supply the aspect 'how should one produce [the fruit].'
Therefore the meaning is: one who desires it should produce heaven by means of the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s> sacrifice.
In both these [Prābhākara and Bhāṭṭa] positions, liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>)—characterized by the self's remaining in its own nature—is also to be obtained by <s>karma</s> (ritual action) alone.
How?
For one who does not perform prohibited actions or even optional (<s>kāmya</s>) actions, due to the absence of causes in the form of merit and demerit, and who is devoid of movement to the upper, lower, and middle worlds which are conditioned [by karma]; for one who performs the obligatory and occasional rites and who, through experiencing the fruits [of past actions], exhausts prior good and bad <s>karmas</s>—for such a sacrificer, the self's remaining in its own nature occurs effortlessly, without any [special] knowledge.
One might object:
If <s>Guru</s> [<s>Prabhākara</s>] and <s>Kumārila</s> are not omniscient—or if they are omniscient—then their statement that the universe is without a Lord is untrustworthy.
In the first case, because of being of limited knowledge; in the second, because it would be a deceptive statement.
Because the <s>Upaniṣadic</s> position is that whoever is omniscient is the Lord himself.
Similarly, the words of <s>Jaimini</s> and <s>Śabarasvāmin</s> worshipped by them are also simply untrustworthy.

Now, if [they say] that only the Lord posited by the logicians (<s>Tārkikas</s>) has been refuted, not the Lord accepted by the <s>Upaniṣads</s>, who is of the nature of the individual self (<s>kṣetrajña</s>)—that is not so.
Because for those who say 'karma alone gives the desired and undesired fruits to embodied beings, not the Lord,' and who accept the <s>Veda</s> as devoted solely to <s>dharma</s>—the Lord, who is of the nature of the individual self, is rendered powerless, and there is no [valid] means of knowledge establishing [such a Lord].
Moreover, [the Mīmāṃsakas] themselves have refuted the Lord's being established through inference, and have demonstrated that scripture is devoted solely to <s>dharma</s>—so what means of knowledge would [the Lord] be based on?
As for the liberation characterized by remaining in one's own nature that was described—is the self previously established in its own nature, or not?
In the first case, liberation is not accomplishable by <s>karma</s>—because the fruit of <s>karma</s> is of the nature of production, attainment, transformation, or purification, and production and the like are impossible for what is already established.
Nor is the second [alternative valid]—because a form that did not previously exist cannot be maintained as [the self's] own nature.
For that which is invariable is called one's own nature.
If liberation were accomplishable by <s>karma</s>, it would not be an eternal human goal—by the principle that whatever is produced is impermanent.
And in the doctrine of an inert self, the stone-like nature or void-like nature of <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation) is inescapable.
As for what is said—that the self is of the nature of substance-cum-consciousness—that too is unsound.
If non-difference between consciousness and unconsciousness is accepted, identity with existence, non-existence, and the like would also follow; and the knowability of cognition through introspective cognition would be unjustified—because of the contradiction between it being the knowable and it being knowledge.
And if introspective cognition is self-established without depending on another, then the prior cognition too could be similarly [self-established].
