Moreover, if knowledge — which is itself unestablished in the <s>ātman</s> (self) — has the capacity to illuminate objects, then objects too should have the capacity to illuminate knowledge, since there is no distinction [between the two cases].
Therefore, the self-luminosity of all cognitions must be accepted.
And since these [cognitions], being specific modifications of the intellect (<s>buddhi</s>), are inert (<s>jaḍa</s>) and hence self-luminosity does not suit them intrinsically — their self-luminous nature must be accepted as [arising] from the proximity of the conscious self (<s>cidātman</s>) alone.
As the <s>śruti</s> (scripture) says: 'Everything shines following That which shines; by Its radiance all this is illuminated.'
As for the removal of the infinite regress defect by establishing the self-sufficiency of difference, taking difference to be a property of the different — that too is not elegant.
Because the difference of properties such as form, taste, and the like from their property-bearers, and from one another, is not established.
Indeed, it is not possible for properties to be the locus of other properties.
Furthermore, is difference among all entities one, or many?
If one — is it inert or non-inert?
If non-inert, it exists in the <s>ātman</s> [alone],
because of the impossibility of the co-ordination of the seen with the seer.
In the second case [if inert], the <s>ātman</s> itself would come to be the referent of the word 'difference,' since there is [only] one all-pervading non-inert entity with that nature.
If [difference is] insentient — does it require another difference, or not?
If it requires [another], there is an infinite regress.
If it does not require [another], then even without depending on difference, the different [entities] themselves, being many, would be [distinct] just like difference.
Therefore, difference — whether as intrinsic nature or as a property — cannot be borne even by <s>Śakra</s> (Indra).
How then [can there be] the difference of the conscious-and-insentient phenomenal world?
Or how [can there be] the difference of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) and the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>)?
Therefore, the doctrine of the <s>Karma-Mīmāṃsakas</s> too should not be adopted by those who seek the highest good. Thus the <s>Brahmavādin</s> (Vedāntin) doctrine is introduced.
The <s>Brahmavādins</s> too are of two kinds: the <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> (Upanishadic) and the <s>Paurāṇikas</s> (Purāṇic).
And the <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> too are of two kinds: those for whom <s>saguṇa Brahman</s> (Brahman with qualities) is primary, and those for whom <s>nirguṇa Brahman</s> (Brahman without qualities) is primary.
page 039

Among them, those for whom <s>saguṇa Brahman</s> is primary are <s>Rāmānuja</s> and others.
Those for whom <s>nirguṇa Brahman</s> is primary are the revered master <s>Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda</s> and others.

<s>Māyā</s>, augmenting <s>saṃsāra</s> through conformity with the fear engendered by the Lord — some, of scanty learning and whose minds are obstructed by fate, have distorted [this teaching]."
Thus.

'Of scanty learning, whose minds are obstructed by fate' — by this, the learned have indicated that their [Rāmānujite] doctrine, having as its root the error regarding the world, soul, and Lord as having no [ultimate] reality, should be disregarded.

body.translated_text:
Among them, for those established in the <s>saguṇa</s> view, the difference of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>), the Lord (<s>Īśvara</s>), and the world (<s>jagat</s>) is real indeed.
<s>Māyā</s> too, being the cause of that [difference] and being a power of the Lord, is real.
Because the reality of powers is observed in real entities such as sesame seeds [which have the power to produce oil].
The conventional designation of 'māyā-ness' regarding it is due to its capacity to accomplish the seemingly impossible — not due to its being unreal.
As the <s>śruti</s> says: '<s>Indra</s>, through his <s>māyās</s>, moves in many forms.'
And there is a difference of that [<s>māyā</s>] for each individual soul. Age after age, the souls desiring liberation, performing hearing, chanting, meditation, and worship of the Lord — who is of the nature of the four emanations (<s>vyūhas</s>) named <s>Vāsudeva</s>, <s>Saṅkarṣaṇa</s>, <s>Pradyumna</s>, and <s>Aniruddha</s> — with devotion and faith preceded [by these], by the grace of the Lord, crossing over His <s>māyā</s> which causes the cycle of birth and other [sufferings], desire liberation in the form of <s>sālokya</s> (residing in the same world), <s>sārūpya</s> (having the same form), <s>sāmīpya</s> (proximity), or <s>sāyujya</s> (union), according to their service.
But those devoid of the Lord's grace, deluded by His <s>māyā</s>, transmigrate here. This is the summary of the established doctrine.
As stated by the authors of the <s>Śārīraka-saṅgraha</s> —
Exposition of the doctrine of the <s>Nirguṇa-Brahmavādins</s> (Advaitins affirming Brahman without qualities).

children.translated_text:
Even in this position, at the conventional level, there are two categories: the seer (<s>dṛk</s>) and the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>).
The seen is <s>Māyā</s>.
The seer is the <s>Puruṣa</s> (Person/Self), who presides over it.
And <s>Māyā</s> is not real — because of being other than the <s>ātman</s> which is real; because of being the cause of a falsely-appearing world, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl; and because of being sublatable by the knowledge of the substratum.
Nor is it unreal — because of being the cause of the universe; and because of its directness [in experience]: 'I do not know myself.'
Nor is it both real and unreal — because existence and non-existence, being of the nature of mutual negation, cannot co-exist in a single locus.
By the method of elimination, it is arrived at that [<s>Māyā</s>] is inexpressible (<s>anirvacenīya</s>).
And it is not different from the <s>ātman</s> — because of the absurd consequence of non-apprehension, and because of the consequence of absolute non-existence.
Nor is it non-different — because of the impossibility of identity between the inert and the non-inert.
Nor is it both different and non-different — because difference and non-difference, being of the nature of mutual negation, cannot undisputedly co-exist in one [entity].
It is not composite (<s>sāvayava</s>) — because of the consequence of being an effect.
It is not without parts (<s>niravayava</s>) — because of being the transformant of the universe.
Nor is it of both natures — because of contradiction.
Therefore, <s>Māyā</s> is simply some power of the Supreme Self, charming so long as it is not investigated.
And it consists of three <s>guṇas</s> (qualities).
<s>Sattva</s>, <s>rajas</s>, and <s>tamas</s> are the <s>guṇas</s>.
And the three-<s>guṇa</s> nature of <s>Māyā</s> [is established] because in the world — its effect — the presence of pleasure, pain, and delusion is observed; and by <s>śruti</s> as well.
This very [<s>Māyā</s>] is called in some places <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance), in some places <s>prakṛti</s> (primordial nature), in some places <s>akṣara</s> (the imperishable), in some places <s>śakti</s> (power), and in some places <s>moha</s> (delusion).
The <s>Vedāntins</s> [hold that] from the proximity of the <s>ātman</s> — possessing that [<s>Māyā</s>] — the five elements beginning with space arise, and from these, presided over by the conscious self, both aggregate and individual bodies are produced.
The <s>Paurāṇikas</s>, however, [hold that] the appearance of duality too is through the reality of the substratum, like [the appearance] of silver.

children.translated_text:
In this position, at the conventional level, there are two categories: the seer (<s>dṛk</s>) and the seen (<s>dṛśya</s>).
The seen is <s>Māyā</s>.
The seer is <s>Puruṣa</s> (the Self).
<s>Māyā</s> is simply some power of the Supreme Self, charming so long as it is not investigated.
And it consists of three <s>guṇas</s>, and is one — as [affirmed by] the <s>śruti</s> beginning with 'the one unborn' (<s>ajām ekām</s>).
The <s>śruti</s> '<s>Indra</s> through his <s>māyās</s>' [which speaks of] its multiplicity is due to the distinction of its parts alone.
This very [<s>Māyā</s>] is designated by terms such as <s>avidyā</s> (ignorance) and others.
From the proximity of the <s>ātman</s> possessing it, the elements beginning with space arise.
From these, bodies both aggregate and individual in form are produced — thus the <s>Vedāntins</s>.

body.translated_text:
For the <s>Aupaniṣadas</s> and <s>Paurāṇikas</s> for whom <s>nirguṇa Brahman</s> is primary — the revered <s>Śaṅkara Bhagavatpāda</s> and others, who hold six-fold or eight-fold means of valid knowledge — in ultimate reality, <s>Brahman</s> alone, of the nature of existence-consciousness-bliss (<s>saccidānanda</s>), is the sole reality.
And it is not the object of any other means of valid knowledge [besides the Veda].
Because the universe, consisting of knower, means of knowledge, and knowable, being superimposed upon it, has no existence apart from it; and being inert by its own nature, its illumination depends on it [Brahman].
Even the non-existence of that [universe] cannot manifest without depending on the conscious self, because of being of a non-luminous nature.
How much less then [can] positive entities like pots and cloths [manifest independently], if the self alone is the reality?
And if it is of undivided nature, whence does the duality consisting of world, soul, and Lord appear?
If it were not a reality, and not a unity, how could the universe appear at all?
Indeed, the establishment of the manifold, inert universe cannot be achieved without accepting one self-luminous reality.
If duality were absolutely non-existent, then whence the appearance of existence?
We say: through the reality of the substratum.
Just as the appearance of the reality of silver [is] through the reality of the mother-of-pearl.
For that [mother-of-pearl], though known merely as 'this is some white, shining thing,' when not known in its own true form, appears to a person who has the impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) of the experience of silver, in the form of silver projected by its own ignorance.
Likewise, the <s>ātman</s> too, though cognized merely as 'I am some luminous substance,' when not known in its own true form as existence-consciousness-bliss, sees in itself the manifold phenomenal world of world, soul, and Lord, projected by self-ignorance.
Exposition of the <s>Paurāṇika</s> (Purāṇic) doctrine.

mahato 'haṃkāraḥ |
sa ca dravyajñānakriyāśaktibhedena trirūpaḥ |

jīvaḥ pramātā |
sa pratyakṣānumānagamyaḥ pratikṣetraṃ māyayā bhinnaḥ |
parameśvarastarkāparaparyāyānumānasahakṛtaśrutipramāṇato nityaśuddhabuddhamuktasvabhāvaḥ sarvajñaḥ sarvaśaktirguṇatrayātmikayā māyayā viśvasṛṣṭisthitisaṃhāratirobhāvānugrahalakṣaṇaiḥ pañcavidhaḥ kṛtyaiḥ svātmanyeva viharati |
sarvakṣetreṣveka eva sthitaḥ san sarvānkṣetrajñānniyamayati ca |
na caikasmin niyāmyaniyāmakabhāvāsaṃbhavaḥ |
māyīyabhedāśrayeṇa tatsaṃbhavāt |
children.translated_text: The individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) is the knower (<s>pramātṛ</s>). It is knowable through perception (<s>pratyakṣa</s>) and inference (<s>anumāna</s>), and is differentiated in each body by <s>māyā</s> (illusion). The Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>), [established] through the authority of <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) assisted by reasoning (<s>tarka</s>) — which is another name for inference — is of the nature of eternal purity, consciousness, and freedom (<s>nityaśuddhabuddhamukta</s>), omniscient (<s>sarvajña</s>), omnipotent (<s>sarvaśakti</s>); through <s>māyā</s> consisting of the three <s>guṇas</s>, he performs the five kinds of divine acts (<s>kṛtya</s>) — characterized as creation (<s>sṛṣṭi</s>), maintenance (<s>sthiti</s>), dissolution (<s>saṃhāra</s>), concealment (<s>tirobhāva</s>), and grace (<s>anugraha</s>) of the universe — within his own self alone. And being the one alone established in all bodies, he governs all embodied knowers (<s>kṣetrajña</s>). Nor is there an impossibility of the relation of controller and controlled in one [entity], because that [relation] is possible through the [apparent] difference based on <s>māyā</s>.
Thus the entire expanse of duality (<s>dvaitaprapañca</s>) is made of <s>māyā</s> (illusion).
<s>Brahman</s> alone, without a second (<s>advitīya</s>), exists in the ultimate sense (<s>paramārthas</s>).
In both these views (i.e. Sāṅkhya-Yoga and Vedānta), since bondage (<s>bandha</s>) is caused by ignorance (<s>avidyā</s>), the cessation of that [ignorance] alone is liberation (<s>mokṣa</s>).

children.text: sa ca 'ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ'; ityādiśrutyā ātmadarśanamanūdya tatsādhanatvena śravaṇādividhānād, vedāntaśravaṇādi kurvato vivekādisādhanasampannasya puṃso bhagavaccaritraśravaṇādibhiḥ pariśodhitāntaḥkaraṇasyāhaṃ brahmāsmīti jīvaparaikyasākṣādbodhe sati sidhyedityakhilamanāvilam ||
children.translated_text: And that [liberation] — by the <s>Śruti</s> (scripture) beginning with 'The Self indeed, O dear one, is to be seen' (<s>ātmā vā are draṣṭavyaḥ</s>), having restated the vision of the Self and having enjoined hearing (<s>śravaṇa</s>) etc. as the means to that — is accomplished for a person who practices <s>Vedānta</s> hearing etc., who is endowed with the means such as discrimination (<s>viveka</s>) etc., whose inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>) has been purified through hearing the accounts of the Lord (<s>Bhagavān</s>) etc., when the direct realization (<s>sākṣādbodha</s>) of the identity of the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) and the Supreme (<s>para</s>) — 'I am <s>Brahman</s>' (<s>ahaṃ brahmāsmi</s>) — arises. Thus [the teaching is] entirely clear and unblemished. ||

body.translated_text:
The <s>Paurāṇikas</s>, however, [hold that] from the Supreme Self imbued with <s>Māyā</s>, [arises] <s>Mahat</s> (the Great Principle).
From <s>Mahat</s>, <s>Ahaṃkāra</s> (Ego).
And that [<s>Ahaṃkāra</s>] is of three forms, due to the distinction of the powers of substance, knowledge, and action.
From the power of substance — from <s>tāmasic Ahaṃkāra</s> — arise the <s>tanmātras</s> (subtle elements) of sound and the rest, and the gross elements beginning with space.
From the power of knowledge — from <s>sāttvic Ahaṃkāra</s> — arise the fourteen deities of the faculties beginning with the quarters, and the inner instruments (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>).
From the power of action — from <s>rājasic Ahaṃkāra</s> — arise the sense organs beginning with hearing, and the organs of action beginning with speech.
All these, from <s>Mahat</s> down to the [gross] elements, impelled by the <s>Puruṣa</s> (Self) who is the wielder of <s>Māyā</s>, coming together with one another, commence the golden egg of <s>Brahmā</s> (<s>Brahmāṇḍa</s>).
And therein arise the fourteen worlds and four kinds of bodies. And in those bodies, the conscious self, which is the cause of all, enters both as witness and as identified ego.
The witness is the Supreme Lord (<s>Parameśvara</s>).
The identified ego is the individual soul (<s>jīva</s>) — as [affirmed by] the <s>śruti</s> beginning with 'Two birds' and the <s>smṛti</s> beginning with 'The Lord of all beings.'
Thus in both these positions, the effect of <s>Māyā</s>, characterized as elemental and physical, is the object of knowledge.
The means of valid knowledge are six or eight, beginning with perception.
